newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Ranbaxy seeks growth outide India.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Ranbaxy seeks growth outide India.

text.p: India's leading pharmaceuticals company Ranbaxy Laboratories plans to curb new investment at its factories in India to concentrate on developing foreign markets, a senior executive said on Wednesday.

Ranbaxy president Davinder Singh Brar told Reuters that the company would slow investments at home in bulk capacities to develop its new markets in Russia, China, Vietnam and the Ukraine, while consolidating its presence in Britain and the United States
"These markets are consolidating...and will be significant players in our overall corporate mix," Brar said in an interview.
Ranbaxy, which earns half of its revenue from exports, said it expected to consolidate its presence in the new markets of Egypt, Poland and Brazil in the next two to three years.
By reducing domestic spending, Ranbaxy hoped to develop its foreign marketing network, increase spending on research and maximise capacity use, Brar said.
Ranbaxy set aside four percent of its revenue for research in 1996-97 and Brar said the intention was to raise it to 5.5 percent by 2000.
The company faces tough competition in the United States in some key drugs which are pending FDA (Food and Drug Administration) approval.
Brar said Ranbaxy hoped to market a version of ranitidine hydrochloride in the United States to compete with Glaxo Wellcome Plc's best-selling anti-ulcer drug Zantac.

He said Ranbaxy was sixth in the queue to launch a generic version of the drug in the United States. But legal proceedings brought by Glaxo to challenge alleged infringements of one of its patents might delay the launch by up to two years.
Zantac is currently the world's best-selling drug and accounted for nearly 30 percent of Glaxo's U.S. sales of 3.68 billion pounds in 1996.

One of two key patents on Zantac expires in July, after which tough competition could lead to an 80 to 85 percent erosion in prices, Brar said. The market could fall to four to five hundred million dollars, he said.
Ranbaxy also intended to introduce a generic version of Aciclovir to compete with another Glaxo drug, the herpes treatment Zovirax, Brar said.

Price erosion triggered by competition and a growing flood of U.S. regulatory approvals of generic products have forced Ranbaxy to reevaluate the operations of its American marketing partner Eli Lilly and Co, Brar said.
"We are trying to understand whether there is a better way to change our product mix, maybe concentrating on niche products where the (price) erosion will not be significant," he said.
By limiting domestic investment, Ranbaxy hopes to keep prices low, something which it has long had to do in the fiercely competitive Indian market.
Brar said its ability to keep a rein on prices had also helped Ranbaxy make strong inroads in the Chinese and Russian anti-infectives markets.
